name: Salicylic Acid
summary: A lipophilic exfoliant that can actually get inside an oily, congested pore — the mechanistic reason it’s favored specifically for blackheads.
good: Blackheads, oily/congested skin, and maintenance-phase pore care.
bad: Layering with a retinoid or another exfoliant in the same routine without spacing — the risk is cumulative irritation, not a specific chemical interaction.
clinicalPearls: Because it’s oil-soluble, salicylic acid reaches inside a clogged, oily pore in a way water-soluble AHAs mostly can’t — that’s the actual reason it outperforms them for blackheads specifically.
mechanism: Lipophilic beta-hydroxy acid that penetrates into the sebaceous follicle and exfoliates keratinocytes lining the pore, reducing comedone formation, with mild anti-inflammatory activity.
originalFields: Lipophilic beta-hydroxy acid that penetrates into the sebaceous follicle and exfoliates keratinocytes lining the pore, reducing comedone formation, with mild anti-inflammatory activity.
Mild comedonal acne (blackheads/whiteheads) and oily, congested skin — usually an adjunct or maintenance step rather than primary inflammatory-acne therapy.
Moderate — several weeks for visible pore and texture improvement.
Low-moderate, concentration-dependent; OTC cleansers/toners are typically low-risk, higher-concentration peels more irritating.
Minimal direct pigment effect; low irritation keeps PIH risk low.
Mild and dose-dependent — can be drying with frequent use at higher concentrations.
Available both ways — wash-off cleansers for gentle daily maintenance, leave-on toners/serums for more active but more drying use.
Either — often part of a cleansing step, so timing is flexible.
A reasonable adjunct to benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid for maintenance, though stacking multiple active exfoliating steps in one routine raises cumulative irritation.
